newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX gasoline ends off highs, stock data doubted.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX gasoline ends off highs, stock data doubted.

text.p: NYMEX gasoline ended higher Wednesday but gave up much of its early gains as dealers looked askance on oil inventory data which suggested unrealistically strong demand amid tightening gasoline supply.
June gasoline ended up 0.61 cent at 60.92 cents a gallon after rising to session high of 61.65 cents.
June crude settled four cents a barrel lower at $19.62 while June heating oil finished 0.45 cent a gallon lower at 53.08 cents.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) said Tuesday evening that gasoline stocks dropped 3.6 million barrels for the week ended May 2. Dealers had been expecting the API to report a build of one to two million barrels.

"We thought demand was overstated and supply was understated. I think it may have something to do with the change to summer (gasoline specifications), so the data may normalize after this," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.

Busby noted refiners may have made their last draw down of winter gasoline to make room for summer gasoline. Summer gasoline is formulated differently to address the smog problem found during the summer.
The draw widened the year-over-year gasoline stock deficit to 13.2 million barrels, the API said.

But, the stock data yielded an implied demand figure for gasoline of 8.7 million barrels per day (bpd) which dealers said was an all-time record. The implied demand made dealers skeptical of the data since they said it is still too early in the driving season to get such high demand.
Dealers also pointed out that cash gasoline values would have been much higher in the New York Harbor and U.S. Gulf last week if demand was as high during that period as the API data suggested.
Dealers said the API data was neutral for crude in that an increase in crude runs of 134,000 bpd somewhat offset a one million barrel rise in stocks. Consequently, prompt crude ended little change.
The data was deemed bearish for heating oil as distillate stocks, composed of heating oil and diesel, rose when dealers had expected a draw due to unseasonably cool weather in the U.S. recently.
